why_use_this: Reach for this package whenever a signal needs to move between the time domain and the frequency domain -- finding what frequencies are present in a sampled waveform, filtering via convolution, or analyzing a system's stability via the Laplace/Z-transform. Use `fft`/`ifft`/`fft_real` (the fast \( O(n\log n) \) Cooley-Tukey path) whenever your data length is a power of 2 -- pad it there first with `next_power_of_two` + `zero_pad`/`zero_pad_complex` if it isn't. Fall back to `dft`/`idft` (the naive \( O(n^2) \) path, any length at all) only when padding to a power of 2 genuinely isn't an option, or as a reference implementation to cross-check `fft` against (which is exactly how this package's own tests validate `fft`'s correctness). Every frequency-domain function works in [vani-complex](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-complex)'s `Complex` type, since a frequency-domain signal is complex-valued in general even when the original time-domain signal is real.

math_notes.dft: The Discrete Fourier Transform: \( X_k = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x_n \, e^{-2\pi i kn/N} \) for \( k=0,\ldots,N-1 \) -- computed directly (naive double loop, \( O(N^2) \)), works for any length \( N \), unlike `fft`.
math_notes.idft: The inverse DFT: \( x_n = \dfrac{1}{N}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} X_k \, e^{+2\pi i kn/N} \) -- the same summation as `dft` with the sign of the exponent flipped and a \( 1/N \) normalization, recovering the original time-domain signal from its frequency-domain representation.
math_notes.fft: The Cooley-Tukey radix-2 Fast Fourier Transform: computes the exact same result as `dft` but in \( O(N\log N) \) instead of \( O(N^2) \), by recursively splitting the DFT of \( N \) points into two DFTs of \( N/2 \) points (even- and odd-indexed samples) and combining them with "twiddle factors" \( e^{-2\pi i k/N} \) -- REQUIRES \( N \) to be a power of 2 for this even/odd split to bottom out exactly.
math_notes.ifft: The inverse FFT -- same Cooley-Tukey radix-2 recursive structure as `fft`, with the sign of the twiddle factors flipped and a final \( 1/N \) scaling, computing the same result as `idft` in \( O(N\log N) \).
math_notes.fft_real: `fft` specialized for real-valued (not complex) input -- since a real signal's DFT is conjugate-symmetric (\( X_{N-k} = \overline{X_k} \)), this still returns the full \( N \)-length complex spectrum (not exploiting the symmetry to save work in this implementation), but saves the caller from having to manually wrap real samples as `Complex` values with zero imaginary part first.
math_notes.dft_magnitude: \( |X_k| = \sqrt{\operatorname{Re}(X_k)^2 + \operatorname{Im}(X_k)^2} \) for every frequency bin -- how much of that frequency is present, discarding phase information.
math_notes.dft_power: \( |X_k|^2 \) for every bin -- the power spectrum, `dft_magnitude` squared (proportional to energy at that frequency, avoiding the square root `dft_magnitude` needs).
math_notes.fft_freq: Maps each output bin index \( k \) to its actual frequency in Hz: \( f_k = k \cdot \text{sample\_rate}/N \) for \( k < N/2 \), and \( f_k = (k-N)\cdot\text{sample\_rate}/N \) (negative) for \( k \ge N/2 \) -- bins past the midpoint represent negative (aliased/wrapped) frequencies, standard FFT output convention.
math_notes.conv_linear: Linear convolution: \( (a * b)_n = \sum_{k} a_k \, b_{n-k} \) -- the direct \( O(nm) \) double-loop definition, output length \( \text{len}(a)+\text{len}(b)-1 \), not FFT-accelerated (fine at this library's modest sizes; FFT-based convolution via the convolution theorem would be the faster route for very long signals).
math_notes.conv_circular: Circular (cyclic) convolution: \( c_m = \sum_k a_k \, b_{(m-k) \bmod n} \) -- like `conv_linear` but wrapping indices modulo \( n \) instead of letting the output grow longer, the convolution that corresponds to pointwise multiplication in the DFT domain (the convolution theorem).
math_notes.correlate: Cross-correlation: like `conv_linear` but WITHOUT time-reversing one of the inputs (convolution flips one signal before sliding; correlation doesn't) -- measures how similar two signals are as a function of the lag between them, commonly used to find a known pattern's location inside a longer signal.
math_notes.window_hann: The Hann window: \( w_i = 0.5\left(1 - \cos\!\dfrac{2\pi i}{n-1}\right) \) for \( i=0,\ldots,n-1 \) -- tapers a signal segment smoothly to zero at both ends before taking its DFT/FFT, reducing spectral leakage (the smearing of a pure tone's energy into neighboring bins caused by analyzing a finite, abruptly-truncated segment).
math_notes.window_hamming: The Hamming window: \( w_i = 0.54 - 0.46\cos\!\dfrac{2\pi i}{n-1} \) -- similar shape to `window_hann` but doesn't taper all the way to zero at the endpoints, trading slightly more spectral leakage for a narrower main lobe in the resulting spectrum.
math_notes.window_blackman: The Blackman window: a 3-term cosine sum \( w_i = 0.42 - 0.5\cos\!\dfrac{2\pi i}{n-1} + 0.08\cos\!\dfrac{4\pi i}{n-1} \) -- a wider main lobe than Hann/Hamming but substantially lower side-lobe leakage, useful when you need to resolve a weak tone next to a much stronger one.
math_notes.window_bartlett: The Bartlett (triangular) window: a straight linear ramp up from 0 to the center and back down to 0, unlike `window_rectangular`'s flat top -- the simplest possible taper, nonzero-sloped but with no cosine shaping.
math_notes.window_kaiser: The Kaiser window: \( w_i = \dfrac{I_0\!\left(\beta\sqrt{1-\left(\tfrac{2i}{n-1}-1\right)^2}\right)}{I_0(\beta)} \), where \( I_0 \) is the zeroth-order modified Bessel function of the first kind -- a single tunable parameter \( \beta \) trades main-lobe width against side-lobe suppression continuously, generalizing the fixed-shape windows above into one adjustable family.
math_notes.window_tukey: The Tukey (tapered-cosine) window: flat (like `window_rectangular`) in the middle, with cosine-tapered edges (like half of `window_hann`) over a fraction \( \alpha \) of the window's length -- interpolates continuously between a rectangular window (\( \alpha=0 \)) and a full Hann window (\( \alpha=1 \)).
math_notes.laplace_transform_numeric: Numerically approximates the (continuous) Laplace transform \( X(s) = \int_0^{\infty} x(t)\,e^{-st}\,dt \) at a single complex frequency \( s \), via numerical integration (trapezoidal-style summation) over the given sampled \( (t,x) \) points rather than a symbolic closed form.
math_notes.z_transform_numeric: Numerically evaluates the (discrete) Z-transform \( X(z) = \sum_{n} x_n \, z^{-n} \) at a single complex point \( z \) -- confirmed in this package's own tests to agree with `dft` when evaluated on the unit circle (\( |z|=1 \), angle \( 2\pi k/n \)), since the DFT is exactly the Z-transform sampled at those specific points.
math_notes.z_transform_inverse: Numerically approximates the inverse Z-transform via the contour-integral formula evaluated on a circle of radius \( r \), recovering the discrete sequence \( x_n \) from samples of \( X(z) \) taken around that circle -- the small imaginary-part residue left over from finite-sample numerical rounding is discarded, since the true inverse of a real sequence's Z-transform is itself real-valued.
